fds-does-not-see-a-room-it-s-cb1451: FDS does not see a room. It sees a box of rectangular cells, and it solves the same set of equations once in every cell, every time step. PyroSim carries the same advice inside the Edit Meshes dialog, where each axis shows a Cell Size Ratio whose tooltip reads "Ratio of this cell dimension to the shortest. what-divisible-by-2-3-and-5-d36604: What "divisible by 2, 3 and 5" actually buys you
pyrosim-warns-when-a-cell-co-38590c: PyroSim warns when a cell count is awkward: "The number of cells is potentially inefficient. a-door-that-does-not-reach-t-8bb4ed: A door that does not reach through the wall is the quietest failure in this whole guide. it-is-about-speed-not-accura-2ed110: It is about speed, not accuracy. why-extend-the-domain-2-4-m-d72371: Why extend the domain 2.4 m past the door instead of putting an OPEN vent across the doorway?
two-reasons-an-open-vent-is-893013: Two reasons. An OPEN vent is only allowed on the exterior boundary of the domain, so one drawn on an interior wall stops the run with ERROR(819). the-fire-is-a-surface-with-a-97d5ff: The fire is a surface with a heat release rate, so today you define the fuel, its smoke, and the ISO 9705 heat output programme
by-the-end-of-today-your-mod-7c27ba: By the end of today your model holds a propane reaction that produces soot and carbon monoxide, and a corner burner that runs 100 kW for ten minutes and then 300 kW for ten more.
there-is-no-fire-object-in-f-5a02f8: There is no fire object in FDS. You do not place a flame. You describe a patch of surface, say how many kilowatts each square metre of it gives off, and FDS pushes fuel gas in through that patch and burns it where it meets oxygen.
so-a-working-burner-needs-tw-90781a: So a working burner needs two separate things, and they live in two separate dialogs. A reaction says what the fuel is and what it turns into. Miss a detail in either one and FDS usually runs to the end and gives you the wrong fire without complaining.
why-a-fire-is-a-boundary-con-170ef0: Why a fire is a boundary condition and not a prediction
fds-solves-the-gas-in-the-ro-bd6223: FDS solves the gas in the room cell by cell. Fuel gas can only enter through the faces of cells, which is why a burner has to be a surface. one-consequence-is-worth-car-6763ec: One consequence is worth carrying into every report you write: this model does not predict how big the fire gets. You prescribe it. Johansson and Ekholm gave eight Swedish consultancies the same problem — an 800 mm heptane pool in a three-room apartment — and compared what came back, in Fire Technology in 2018. In their words, the differences in how the fuel and the burner were described were relatively large, which resulted in large differences in mass loss rate and heat release rate. The room physics was the easy part. The burner definition was where the answers diverged.
the-reaction-and-the-trap-in-86ed1f: The reaction, and the trap in the library
from-fds-6-onward-a-reaction-ef6159: From FDS 6 onward a reaction is compulsory for a fire, and the guide is explicit that you are responsible for the fuel chemistry and for the post-combustion yields of CO and soot, because those yields default to zero. pyrosim-ships-a-property-lib-2c1f75: PyroSim ships a property library with 21 predefined entries named FDS6 PROPANE, FDS6 METHANE and so on. Each of those entries sets the fuel and nothing else. set-two-numbers-on-the-bypro-c7ea19: Set two numbers on the Byproducts tab and the problem goes away: a soot yield of 0.024 and a CO yield of 0.005, both in kilograms per kilogram of fuel burned. what-those-two-yields-do-and-4055eb: What those two yields do and do not change
the-yields-are-fractions-of-7cd96a: The yields are fractions of fuel mass: 0.024 means 24 g of soot for every kilogram of propane burned. They apply to well-ventilated, post-flame conditions, which is what a 100 kW and 300 kW burner in an open-doored room gives you.

the-surface-and-the-arithmet-e2db50: The surface, and the arithmetic that decides your fire
a-burner-surface-carries-one-839be1: A burner surface carries one number that matters today: heat release rate per unit area, in kW/m². Run it backwards to get what you type: divide the kilowatts you want by the square metres of burner top.
the-iso-9705-ignition-source-7958e7: The ISO 9705 ignition source is a 170 mm square sand burner, so its top is 0.17 × 0.17 m = 0.0289 m². Your mesh cannot draw that. drawn-as-0-2-0-2-m-on-the-gr-753b97: Drawn as 0.2 × 0.2 m on the grid
the-0-2-m-patch-is-a-modelli-5a1789: The 0.2 m patch is a modelling choice, not part of the standard, and you should say so whenever you report the case. the-programme-and-the-two-wa-943047: The programme, and the two ways to ramp
iso-9705-1-2016-clause-6-4-s-cea327: ISO 9705-1:2016 clause 6.4 sets the heat output: 100 kW for the first 10 minutes after ignition, then 300 kW for a further 10 minutes. That is 600 s and 1200 s, and it is why the reference run is 1200 s long.
fds-will-not-step-from-nothi-12cebf: FDS will not step from nothing to full output instantly unless you insist. a-time-constant-in-the-fds-f-03c3a6: A time constant. In the FDS file this is TAU_Q. A positive value gives the tanh curve above. A negative value gives a t-squared growth that reaches full output at the absolute value of the number and holds it there: TAU_Q=-300 means full output at 300 s. a-custom-ramp-a-list-of-time-f4d654: A custom ramp. A list of (time, fraction) pairs. the-two-are-mutually-exclusi-4d73bc: The two are mutually exclusive. The FDS User's Guide says so in section 11.1: the TAUs and the RAMPs cannot both be used on the same quantity. one-last-decision-before-you-d74bc5: One last decision before you draw anything: how high the burner sits. the-first-division-to-unders-de9098: The first division to understand is gas-phase against solid-phase. A gas-phase device measures a property of the air in a cell, and PyroSim's own documentation is blunt about what that means: the value is taken at the cell centre, regardless of where in the cell you place the device. A solid-phase device measures a property of a surface, and is taken at a cell face; it needs a Normal of Solid so FDS knows which way the surface points.
why-the-position-inside-a-ce-3213d8: Why the position inside a cell does not matter
the-fds-user-s-guide-states-9c6b6c: The FDS User's Guide states it directly: FDS uses the device coordinates only to decide which cell the device is in, then reads that cell's centred or face-centred value, and no interpolation is done. So on 10 cm cells a ceiling device typed at 2.35 m and one typed at 2.31 m return identical numbers, because both sit in the cell spanning 2.30 to 2.40 m. Change to 20 cm cells and the same device reads the centre of the 2.20 to 2.40 m cell instead — 2.30 m. The device did not move; the cell did.
a-device-sitting-exactly-on-3d753d: A device sitting exactly on a cell boundary is assigned to the cell with the greater coordinate. Thunderhead's tutorial adds a practical warning for solid-phase devices: put the horizontal position inside one cell rather than on a corner, because at a corner FDS will in effect pick one of the four adjoining cells.
the-second-division-is-tempe-4cbc8f: The second division is TEMPERATURE against THERMOCOUPLE, and it catches almost everyone. TEMPERATURE is the gas temperature in the cell. THERMOCOUPLE is the temperature of a modelled metal bead sitting in that cell, which absorbs and re-radiates heat and takes time to warm up. The guide's own words are that the thermocouple temperature lags the true gas temperature by an amount set mainly by its bead size. In a short verification run on this project's Mac, a 20 kW burner in a 1 m box gave 172.6 °C for TEMPERATURE and 84.8 °C for THERMOCOUPLE at the same point at the same instant. Neither is wrong. They are different instruments.
what-the-bead-model-actually-731032: What the bead model actually solves, and its defaults
fds-writes-an-energy-balance-829500: FDS writes an energy balance on a small sphere: convection from the gas, plus absorbed radiation, minus what the bead re-radiates, divided by the bead's mass and specific heat. In FDS 6.10.1 — the version PyroSim 2026.1 bundles — the defaults are a bead diameter of 0.001 m, an emissivity of 0.85, and the density and specific heat of nickel, 8908 kg/m³ and 0.44 kJ/(kg·K). PyroSim exposes all four as Bead Diameter, Emissivity, Bead Density and Bead Specific Heat.
fds-6-11-1-changed-those-las-7e47ca: FDS 6.11.1 changed those last two to Type-K values, 8700 kg/m³ with a specific heat that ramps from 0.4515 kJ/(kg·K) at 20 °C to 0.6010 kJ/(kg·K) at 1200 °C. You are not running 6.11.1, so you get nickel. If you later compare against a paper that used a newer FDS, that is one place the two can differ.
the-rule-of-thumb-that-follo-b32c02: The rule of thumb that follows: if you are emulating a real thermocouple or a real detector, use THERMOCOUPLE. If you want the gas temperature a zone model or a hand correlation would predict, use TEMPERATURE. Do not mix the two inside one channel, and whenever you quote a temperature, say which of the two it came from.
gases-are-not-separate-quant-cd1e11: Gases are not separate quantities in FDS 6. Carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide and oxygen are all read with the quantity VOLUME FRACTION plus a SPEC_ID naming the species: 'CARBON MONOXIDE', 'CARBON DIOXIDE', 'OXYGEN'. There is no OXYGEN VOLUME FRACTION quantity in FDS 6, so a menu entry that reads like one is showing you a label, not a keyword. Volume fraction comes out in mol/mol, so a reading of 0.000061 is 61 ppm: ppm is mol/mol multiplied by 1,000,000.
getting-ppm-out-of-pyrosim-r-d5a31b: Getting ppm out of PyroSim rather than out of a spreadsheet
fds-can-do-the-multiplicatio-b1c823: FDS can do the multiplication for you. The &DEVC keywords are CONVERSION_FACTOR=1.0E6 with UNITS='ppm', and that is exactly what the reference case uses, so its CO columns are already in ppm with ppm in the units row of the CSV. The research notes for this guide do not record a PyroSim dialog field that writes those two keywords, so on the office desktop assume you will either multiply mol/mol by 1,000,000 when you read the CSV, or add the keywords to the exported .fds file on Day 7. Whichever you choose, write the choice down: a CO channel that is silently in mol/mol and one that is in ppm differ by six orders of magnitude and both look plausible in a plot.
one-more-prerequisite-from-d-f13257: One more prerequisite, from Day 3: CO and soot only exist in the run if you set CO_YIELD and SOOT_YIELD on the reaction. Both default to zero. With them at zero a CO device does not error: the 1 m test box on this project's Mac, run once with the yields left out, returned CO exactly 0, optical density 0 and visibility pinned at its 30 m maximum for the whole run.
smoke-is-measured-three-ways-30906b: Smoke is measured three ways and they are related by constants you can look up. FDS tracks an extinction coefficient K, computed as the mass extinction coefficient times the soot mass per unit volume. OPTICAL DENSITY is K divided by 2.3, in units of 1/m — this is the quantity DATASET consumes. VISIBILITY is a visibility factor C divided by K, in metres.
what-changes-if-you-alter-it-620952: What changes if you alter it
scales-k-so-it-moves-optical-a2188f: Scales K, so it moves optical density and visibility together. The suggested value for flaming fuels, quoted with an uncertainty of about ±1100 m²/kg at 633 nm.
only-visibility-3-is-a-light-77a6b4: Only visibility. 3 is a light-reflecting sign, 8 is a light-emitting sign.
the-ceiling-on-the-reported-5a4388: The ceiling on the reported visibility. FDS cannot report infinity, so clear air reads exactly this number.
the-visibility-factor-is-wor-5a8999: The visibility factor is worth one experiment before you trust any visibility number. Two identical runs on this project's Mac, one at C = 3 and one at C = 8, gave the same optical density to four figures — 0.3385 1/m — and visibilities of 3.855 m and 10.280 m. The ratio is 2.667, which is 8 divided by 3, everywhere the reading is below the 30 m cap. So switching that one field multiplies every uncapped visibility by 2.67 without a single molecule of smoke changing. Optical density is untouched by it, which is one good reason DATASET's wire contract asks for optical density per metre rather than visibility.
a-smoke-layer-is-not-somethi-831177: A smoke layer is not something FDS computes. It is a two-zone construct, and FDS reconstructs it after the fact by integrating temperature along one vertical line — the method of Janssens and Tran. The New Layer Zoning Device entry gives you that line, with three tick boxes: Measure Layer Height, Upper Temperature and Lower Temperature. Both ends of the path must lie in the same mesh.
how-to-read-a-layer-height-t-00e6cf: How to read a layer height that is not moving
fds-integrates-the-temperatu-af38ec: FDS integrates the temperature and its reciprocal up the line, solves for an interface height, and reports the upper and lower averages in °C. Solid cells in the column are skipped. The behaviour worth memorising is the fallback: if the computed upper-layer temperature is less than 1 K above the temperature of the lowest cell on the line, FDS returns the full length of the line as the layer height. In a 2.4 m room with the line running floor to ceiling, that is a flat 2.4 m.
so-a-layer-height-pinned-at-bc20c7: So a layer height pinned at exactly the line length is FDS saying "I cannot find a layer here", not "the layer is at the ceiling". On the Mac verification run a corner line of length 1.0 m read 1.0 m for its whole three seconds, for that reason. Layer height is also measured from the lower end of the line, so start the line at z = 0 m if you want heights above the floor.
last-fed-fractional-effectiv-40a09b: Last, FED — fractional effective dose. It is a device-only quantity; you cannot make a slice of it. More importantly, the FED device is always a running time integral from the start of the simulation, whatever averaging you ask for. FDS forces that internally. A FED column therefore never falls, and a FED value has no meaning without the time it belongs to. FDS's FED is the asphyxiant model: a carbon monoxide dose multiplied by a carbon dioxide hyperventilation factor, plus a separate oxygen-depletion dose, and no thermal term at all. A reaction with no CO yield leaves only the oxygen term, and heat never enters the number. The FED Activity level is 1 at rest, 2 doing light work, 3 doing heavy work, and the default is 2.
dataset-consumes-three-channe-587f40: DATASET consumes three channels per zone: temperature_c in °C, optical_density as OD per metre, and co_ppm in ppm. Occupancy is the fourth channel and it comes from the crowd simulator, never from FDS — a frame carrying a channel from the wrong owner is rejected. Each zone's physical node is one box holding a K-type thermocouple read through a MAX31855, a photoelectric obscuration chamber that reports OD per metre directly, and an electrochemical CO cell. Three devices at one point emulate that node.
the-node-s-mounting-height-i-b96640: The node's mounting height is not written down anywhere in the DATASET knowledge base, so this guide follows the reference case and puts the emulated node in the topmost cell, at 2.35 m in a 2.4 m room, where a detector would sit. The quantities that say how survivable the room is — visibility, which DATASET predicts alongside temperature and CO, and FED, oxygen and carbon dioxide, which you use to check it — go at head height, 1.85 m. Two positions: S1 at the room centre and S2 near the door, so you can see how much a node's reading depends on where in the room it hangs.

those-are-the-tenability-qua-cb47c1: Those are the tenability quantities from the same 20 cm run: visibility and the FED integral at head height, and the heat flux arriving at the floor centre. With the soot yield at zero, visibility sits at its 30 m maximum for the whole run; with the CO yield at zero, the FED integral barely moves; with the walls left on the default INERT surface, which is fixed at the ambient temperature, the floor flux reads low.
a-device-placed-outside-ever-600fd0: A device placed outside every mesh does not stop the run and does not raise an error. FDS prints one line to the console — WARNING: DEVC S2_T is not within any mesh. — skips the device, finishes normally and reports STOP: FDS completed successfully. The only visible symptom is that the column is missing from CHID_devc.csv. On this project's Mac a test case with two devices, one of them outside the mesh, produced a CSV whose header held a single name. If you are generating hundreds of runs on Day 7, a mistyped coordinate silently costs you a channel in every one of them. Read the console log for WARNING: DEVC before you trust a batch, and count the columns in the CSV against the devices in the model.
a-related-silence-a-solid-ph-eca3f9: A related silence: a solid-phase device on a wall that still has the default INERT surface reads ambient, flat, for the entire run — the reserved surface INERT is fixed at the ambient temperature by definition. Thunderhead's own tutorial teaches this with a ceiling that sits at a constant 22 °C from start to finish.
